en: The original title of *Jiaoguan Gangzong* was *Yidai Shijiao Quanshi Gangyao Tu*. As a long scroll, it was difficult to view. Now, I have added the ten-vehicle contemplations for each of the four teachings and reformatted it as a bound volume, titled *Beitianmu Oyi Shamen Zhixu Chongshu Fozu Zhi Yao Jiaogan Erji* (The Essential Teachings and Contemplations of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, Re-stated by the Bhikṣu Zhixu of Northern Tianmu).
Contemplation is not correct without teaching; teaching is not [complete] without contemplation.
It is not transmitted.
To have the teaching without contemplation leads to delusion;
to have contemplation without the teaching leads to peril.
However, when considering the temporal teachings as a whole,
there are eight general outlines.
Based on these teachings, one establishes the contemplations.
The enumeration is also roughly the same.
As for the eight teachings:
first, the sudden; second, the gradual; third, the secret; and fourth, the indeterminate.
These are called the four teachings of the transformative ritual.

They correspond to the worldly medical prescriptions: (1) the Tripitaka, (2) the Shared, (3) the Distinct, and (4) the Perfect. Furthermore, there are (5) the five supernormal powers, (6) the six supernormal powers, (7) the distinct [teachings], and (8) the perfect [teachings].
These are called the four teachings of the transformative Dharma.
Just as with the flavors of worldly medicines,
one should understand how they are applied in the case of the sudden and other approaches.
In total, they do not go beyond the four flavors, such as the *pitaka* [Tripitaka] and so forth.

The *pitaka* takes the analytical emptiness (*prabheda-śūnyatā*) as its contemplation; the *samdhāya-bhāṣita* (Shared Teaching) takes the essential emptiness (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) as its contemplation.
The sequential [approach] takes successive stages as its contemplation;
the perfect [approach] takes the single mind as its contemplation.
Each of these four contemplations employs ten dharmas to constitute a vehicle capable of transporting the practitioner to the stage of nirvana.
The contemplations of the two teachings— the Tripitaka and the Shared—
convey one to the Nirvana of the True Truth; the contemplations of the two teachings— the Distinct and the Perfect— [convey one to the Nirvana of the Middle Way].
When transported to the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Middle Truth,
the three— Tripitaka, Shared, and Distinct—
are all termed provisional.
Only the contemplation of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) is termed "true and real.
Within this Perfect Contemplation, there are further three categories:
first, the sudden; second, the gradual; and third, the indeterminate.
When the provisional is practiced for the sake of the real, the provisional contains the real;
when the provisional is opened, the real is revealed.
Thus, the ultimate reality is harmonized with skillful means;
this is truly because the faculties and natures of sentient beings are not uniform,
which causes the Tathāgata to teach with diverse skillful methods.
Furthermore, to provide a brief judgment regarding one lifetime [of the Buddha's teaching], there are five periods.
First is the Avataṃsaka period.
[The following is] the general diagram of the provisional and real aspects of the five periods and eight teachings.
Regarding the teaching, it is termed "sudden" (dun) in terms of the method of conversion.
Second, the period of the Āgamas.
It speaks only of the Tripiṭaka teaching;
in terms of the method of conversion, it is called the initial gradual [teaching].
Next is the time of the Vaipulya.
Regarding the gate of arising and ceasing of the "half-syllables" in the Tripiṭaka teachings,
it is contrasted with the gate of non-arising and non-ceasing of the "full-syllables" in the Śāstra teachings of the Shared, Distinct, and Perfect Teachings;
in terms of the ritual of conversion, this is called the gradual.
Fourth, during the period of Prajñāpāramitā,
while retaining both the provisional principles of the Shared and Distinct Teachings,
it correctly expounds the true principle of the Perfect Teaching.
In terms of the method of transformation, it is called "gradual" and occurs later;
during the periods of the five dharmas, the Lotus Sūtra, and the Nirvāṇa Sūtra,
the Lotus Sūtra reveals the provisional [teachings] of the common and distinct aspects of the Three Piṭakas.
It reveals exclusively the reality of the Perfect Teaching,
profoundly clarifies the beginning and end of the Tathāgata’s establishment of the teachings,
and fully unfolds the vastness and profundity of the Tathāgata’s original and manifested traces.
In terms of the method of transformation, it is called "gradual convergence toward the sudden," and is also termed "neither sudden nor gradual.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* was preached again for those who had not yet entered the reality.
He spoke extensively on the eternal nature [of reality],
and furthermore, for the sake of those with dull faculties in the final age,
he repeatedly supported the three provisional teachings.
Therefore, we retrospectively explain the four teachings and retrospectively dissolve the four teachings;
according to the ritual of transformation, this is also termed "neither sudden nor gradual."
Furthermore, while the two modes of transformation— the esoteric and the indefinite—
pervade the aforementioned four periods,
only the Lotus Sūtra is manifest.
Therefore, it is not secret;
because it is definitive,
it is not indeterminate.
However, these five periods have both specific and general aspects; therefore,
one must use the specific to determine the general, and subsume the general into the specific.
This shall ensure that the teachings and contemplations are all clearly distinguished without confusion.
First, I present the diagram of the five periods and eight teachings;
next, I set forth the discourse on the five periods in terms of both the general and the specific.
Regarding the General and Specific Treatises on the Five Periods: one should first understand that these are most appropriate for the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra).
It states: "Now, as for the discussion of the five flavors and the half and full [teachings], the specific [teachings] have their own limits."
The *Lun Tong* applies to both the beginning and the end.
The Venerable Zhiyi said:
"People say..."
In the second period,
for twelve years, he taught the distinct doctrines of the three vehicles.
If that were so, then after the twelve years had passed...
There are those who ought to hear of the Four Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and the Six Perfections;
how could these not be taught?
If they were taught, the Three Vehicles would not be restricted to a period of twelve years.
If it were not taught, then for those who ought to hear it, that single section remaining at the end—
how could the Buddha fail to transform them?
Certainly, such a principle does not exist.
The Sūtra says:
"For the sake of the śrāvakas, he taught the Four Noble Truths,
and so on, up to the Six Perfections."
It was not merely twelve years; rather,
throughout the course of his life,
he taught whatever was appropriate for those who heard him.
The four Āgamas and the five divisions of the Vinaya are taught for the sake of the śrāvakas,
continuing until the final passing of the Sage.
This is precisely the matter at hand.
How can it be said that the Hīnayāna [teachings] were all completed within twelve years? Others say:
The third period:
during thirty years, he taught the Prajñāpāramitā, the Vimalakīrti, and the Saṃdhinirmocana according to the school of emptiness (śūnyatāvāda).
On what scriptural passage is it known that this lasted for thirty years?
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Subhūti, within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*..."
I have heard it said that even raising a hand or bowing the head can lead one to become a Buddha;
for this reason, I now inquire about the meaning of "retrogression. If this is so, [then...]
Regarding the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,
what determines their chronological order?

The wise Zhiyi and Zhizhe [Zhang'an] have clarified this matter as such; yet nowadays,
people do not deign to cast even a glance upon it.
Furthermore, the false claims that the Āgamas consist of twelve divisions and the Vaipulya sūtras consist of eight divisions have been erroneously transmitted;
their harm is extremely great.
Therefore, I shall first present a general discussion to clarify this.
Next, I shall present a specific discussion.
First, regarding those who penetrate all five periods:
there is a certain class of beings with great capacity.
To see, within this very land,
the body and land of Śākyamuni in the Flower Treasury World as eternally abiding and imperishable is the Avataṃsaka Sūtra’s penetration of the future limit.
The current *Huayan* scripture’s "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter likewise does not fall within the three-week period; furthermore,
there is another class of practitioners with limited capacity.
From the beginning at the Deer Park until the end at the Śāla Grove,
one hears only the Āgamas, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma;
thus, it is clear that the Tripiṭaka extends throughout both the earlier and later periods.
Zhang’an has thus refuted [this view];
why do these deluded people still persist in their confusion?
Furthermore, there is another class of those with limited capacities.
They ought to hear the censure and praise [of their conduct] so as to give rise to shame and aspiration.
The Buddha then preached for them the Vaipulya Dharma-gates;
how could it be restricted to the period after twelve years, lasting only eight years?
Furthermore, for instance, the Fangdeng tuoluoni jing (Vaipulya Dhāraṇī Sūtra) is said to follow after the Fahua jing (Lotus Sūtra); thus,
it is clear that the Vaipulya class also extends across both the earlier and later periods.
Furthermore, there are those of the three vehicles who must traverse the mundane and supramundane dharmas, such as form and mind;
each of these eventually converges upon the path of the Mahāyāna.
The Buddha then teaches them the Prajñāpāramitā.
Therefore it is said:
from the initial attainment of the Way until nirvāṇa,
throughout that interval, he constantly preached the Prajñāpāramitā.
Thus, it is clear that Prajñā-pāramitā also extends throughout both the preceding and the subsequent [teachings].
Furthermore, for those sentient beings whose faculties have matured,
the Buddha immediately reveals the provisional to manifest the ultimate for them.
The provisional traces are opened to reveal the fundamental reality;
there is certainly no principle that [the Buddha] would withhold [this revelation] until forty years later.
It is simply that the Buddha, by means of his supernatural powers...
Thus, those whose faculties are not yet mature do not hear it.
Therefore, the Great Master Zhi said:
"The Lotus Sūtra pertains to the aspect of the manifest teaching."
It is not seen before one;
this is the discourse on the secret limits.
In principle, there is no obstruction.
Furthermore, as the sutra says:
"In the past, I heard such a Dharma from the Buddha,
seeing various bodhisattvas receiving the prediction of their future buddhahood."
If such is the Dharma,
is it not indeed the Sublime Dharma?
Furthermore, the Brahmajāla Sūtra says:
"I have now come to this world eight thousand times;
sitting upon the Vajra-flower Radiance King Throne and so forth—
is this not also the opening of the traces to reveal the fundamental?"
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who are to be delivered by seeing the Buddha enter nirvana; for them,
the Buddha immediately manifests the entry into nirvana.
Therefore it is said:
within each of the eight phases,
there are eight inconceivable phases.
Furthermore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* recounts the circumstances of King Ajātaśatru’s repentance and so forth;
these were certainly not events that occurred within a single day and night.
Next, to clarify the distinct five periods:
this refers to a certain class of the most dull-witted śrāvakas,
who must undergo five successive cycles of refinement.
Only then does one enter the reality;
that is to say, at first, within the *Avataṃsaka*, there was neither seeing nor hearing.
This is the stage of "complete birth," which is like milk, occurring prior to the first eight assemblies of the *Avataṃsaka*.
There are never any śrāvakas;
therefore, it is said that they neither see nor hear [the Buddha].
This continues until the ninth assembly, the "Entry into the Dharma Realm" chapter.
Within the Jeta Grove,
there were then śrāvakas who had already realized the fruits of sainthood.
Regarding the realm of the Bodhisattvas,
they are like the mute and the deaf;
this may be verified and known.
Even if you had previously heard the Avataṃsaka Sūtra,
it certainly would have been of no benefit.
However, Śāriputra and the others—
Only by hearing the teachings of the Pitakas can one realize the fruits of sainthood and enter the assembly of the Dharma-realm.
Thus we know that the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter must have been composed after the Āgamas were finalized; it cannot be said to have existed prior to them.
Why do people fail to reflect and examine this at all?

They falsely claim that the *Avataṃsaka* is restricted to the three seven-day periods [of the Buddha's illness], and subsequently, upon hearing the teaching of dependent origination and the law of arising and ceasing in the *Āgamas*, [they dismiss it].
Transforming the mundane into the sacred is like transforming milk into curd— curd being the thickened juice of mature milk— and subsequently hearing the Vaipulya (fangděng) teachings,
which censure the partial and disparage the small while praising the Great and extolling the Perfect.
Consequently, he felt ashamed of his minor aspirations and yearned for the Great [Vehicle].
He lamented his own status as a "ruined seed," even though he had fully heard the four teachings.
However, they secretly obtain general benefit,
just as when curd is transformed into fresh butter;
next, they hear the Prajñāpāramitā.
They realize that all dharmas are the Mahāyāna;
they instruct and transform bodhisattvas,
and they take charge of and understand the precious treasury of all Buddha-dharmas.
Although it encompasses both the general and the specific,
it primarily elucidates the Perfect Teaching;
yet, one only secretly attains its specific benefits.
Just as fresh butter is refined into matured ghee,
one next hears the Lotus Sūtra,
which reveals the ultimate reality by opening up the provisional means.
Only then can one obtain the true benefit of the Perfect Teaching (Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa),
which is like transforming matured ghee into *sarpis* (clarified butter).
Nevertheless, this alone constitutes the distinct teaching of the five periods.
Nor is it restricted by fixed months, years, days, or times;
rather, whenever one is ready to hear,
one immediately hears it.
When the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma,
his supernormal powers are sovereign; with a single voice, beings understand it differently according to their own dispositions.
How could this be subject to conceptual calculation?
Furthermore, there are those whose faculties are somewhat sharp who need not necessarily pass through all five flavors.
Or, by undergoing refinement through only four, three, or two rounds,
one may immediately enter the reality.
This applies to the Āgamas, the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtras), and the Prajñāpāramitā.
Those who enter [the path] through one [of these means] are subsumed under the two types of transformative methods: the esoteric and the indeterminate.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings...
Those who are unable to hear the Lotus Sutra may either willingly withdraw from their seats or be transported to other realms.
This, then, must await the gathering-in [of remains] at the time of nirvana,
or await another Buddha after his parinirvāṇa;
such matters are not uniform.
If you thoroughly study the *Fahua xuanyi* and the *Wenju*,
the multitude of doubts will be resolved of themselves.
Regarding the four teachings of the provisional transformation (*huayi*), there are two meanings for the teaching of the sudden (*dun*).
First is the Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao) school.
This refers to that which was taught suddenly for those of great capacity immediately after his initial attainment of enlightenment;
it is restricted solely to the *Avataṃsaka* within the entirety of his lifetime's teachings.
This refers directly to the Great Dharma outside the realms,
which is not shared with the three vehicles,
such as the Brahmajāla Sūtra, the Complete Enlightenment Sūtra (Awakening of Faith), and others.
It is also appropriate to include [these teachings] within this section.
This is called "using the specific to determine the general," whereby the general is subsumed into the specific. This is the second characteristic of the Sudden Teaching.
This refers to the meaning that at the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one attains perfect awakening;
and that the nature and cultivation are non-dual, such that the essence of the sentient being and the Buddha are equal.
This is precisely the teaching of the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā sūtras.
All of these are present therein.
"Gradual" (jìan) also has two meanings:
first, the category of gradual teaching (jiànjiào bù).
That is to say, those teachings that are restricted solely to the Āgamas— namely, the gradual initial stage for ordinary beings within a single lifetime,
including the doctrines of arising and ceasing, the Four Noble Truths, the twelvefold dependent origination, the six perfections, and so forth—
all such provisional dharmas of the Three Vehicles should be subsumed under this Vaipulya division as the gradual middle stage for ordinary beings within a single lifetime.
The sūtras spoken that criticize the partial and disparage the small while praising the great and extolling the perfect,
as well as those not subsumed within the other four periods,
should all be included in this division.
Since the scope of the term "dominant condition" (adhipati-pratyaya) is broad, all the teachings on *prajñā*— whether common or uncommon—
expounded throughout the course of a single lifetime, including those of the gradual [vehicle],
should be subsumed within this section as the two characteristics of the gradual teaching.
That is to say, regarding the sequence of practicing through successive kalpas, severing delusions,
and realizing the stages of attainment, the *Avataṃsaka* likewise possesses this.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* brings the gradual back to the sudden.
It is not sudden because it differs from the initial teaching of the Avataṃsaka;
nor is it gradual because it differs from the Āgamas, Vaipulya, and Prajñāpāramitā sūtras, which remain sequential and have not yet been integrated.
Therefore, it is not gradual;
yet it still simultaneously illuminates both the sudden and the gradual aspects.
Furthermore, "esoteric" also carries two meanings.
First, the Secret Teaching:
this refers to teaching those individuals the sudden [approach] during any of the aforementioned four periods.
For these people, he taught the gradual [vehicle] and so forth;
they were unaware of one another, each attaining benefit for themselves.
Now, with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*’s directness, he abandons expedient means.
It speaks only of the unsurpassed path;
therefore, it is not a secret mantra of the two secrets,
meaning all dharani phrases and sentences.
That is to say, it is present throughout all five periods of the teaching. Furthermore,
the "indeterminate" [teaching] also possesses two meanings.
First, the indeterminate teaching:
this refers to when, among the aforementioned four periods,
one teaches that person all at once.
For such persons, one teaches the gradual path;
thus they come to know one another,
and each attains their respective benefit.
That is to say, those who are suited to hear the sudden teaching hear the sudden, while those suited to hear the gradual teaching hear the gradual.
Since the *Lotus Sūtra* definitively expounds the Mahāyāna, it is not a teaching of indeterminate characteristics; nor is there any benefit that is indeterminate.
This means that during the first four periods, one may obtain gradual benefit from hearing the sudden teaching,
or obtain sudden benefit from hearing the gradual teaching;
this is precisely using the sudden to assist the gradual.

This means that the gradual [teaching] assists the sudden; for upon hearing even a single phrase or a single verse of the *Lotus Sūtra*, one immediately receives the prediction of attaining Buddhahood.
Thus, it is not the case that the benefit is indefinite. This concludes the section on the Sudden Teaching.
The Gradual Teaching school employs only two types of transformative methods, namely the Perfect and the Distinct;
it fully utilizes all four types of transformative methods.
The manifest and indeterminate [bodies] pervade all four periods and likewise employ the four kinds of transformative methods.
The secret and indeterminate [teachings] likewise pervade the four periods;
they also employ the four kinds of transformative methods— the characteristics of the Sudden Teaching.
The distinction lies solely in the term "perfect" (yuan). If one considers them comprehensively,
even the first three teachings each possess their own sense of the sudden (dun).
The gradual teaching aspect, such as that of those who attain arhatship through the "Welcome" (svāgata) method and so forth,
is restricted to the Tripitaka, Shared, and Distinct Teachings.
Generally speaking, the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) also possesses the sense of gradual progression,
such as the stages of contemplative practice (guanxing), semblance realization (xiangsi), partial realization (fenzheng), and ultimate realization (jiujing).
This refers to the Esoteric Teaching (mimijiao).
Because they do not know one another,
there is nothing that can be transmitted.
This is the secret mantra.
In accordance with the four *siddhāntas*,
there is that which can be transmitted: the teaching of non-fixity.
The indeterminate benefits are all included within the aforementioned four periods;
therefore, there is no separate division to be pointed out. Furthermore, regarding the ritual of transformation and the teaching, three contemplations are established.
This refers to instantaneous contemplation, gradual contemplation, and indeterminate contemplation;
as these constitute the Esoteric Teachings,
they cannot be transmitted.
Therefore, it is not possible to establish a fixed contemplation based upon them. Even if one were to establish a contemplation,
it would merely be that these three methods— sudden, gradual, and indeterminate— are all secret.
Now, regarding these three contemplations,
their names and teachings are the same,
yet their essential meaning is vastly different.
Why is this so? The Sudden Teaching refers to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; its meaning, however, encompasses both the distinct and the universal.
Sudden contemplation applies exclusively to those of the Perfect Teaching;
it involves contemplating the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena from the very first moment of the initial mind,
as is clearly explained in the *Mohe zhiguan* (The Great Calming and Contemplation).
The gradual teaching refers to the Āgamas, Vaipulya, and Prajñāpāramitā;
its meaning encompasses the four teachings,
yet it has not yet revealed the ultimate truth.
Gradual contemplation also applies exclusively to those of the Perfect Teaching;
although their understanding is already complete,
their practice must proceed through successive stages.
This is as clarified in the Dharma-gate explaining the *dhyānapāramitā*.
"Indeterminate teaching" refers to the preceding four periods.
It also encompasses the four teachings,
yet they have not been unified;
it is the contemplation of the indeterminate.
This also applies exclusively to those of the Perfect type,
whose understanding is already perfect;
regardless of which practice they follow, [it is effective].
Whether by skipping stages or following them in sequence,
all may attain realization and entry,
as clarified in the *Six Sublime Gates* (Ṣaḍ-anupūrva-vihāra). This original manuscript was preserved in the kingdom of Koguryo.
In China, these have been lost.
If one asks why it is sufficient to speak only of the Perfect and Sudden *śamatha-vipaśyanā*,
what is the intention behind further explaining the Gradual and the Indeterminate?
Answer: The faculties and dispositions of sentient beings are each distinct.
If one were to speak only of sudden enlightenment, it would fail to encompass all capacities.
Question: Since you have already mentioned the gradual and the indeterminate approaches, why do you refer exclusively to the person of the Perfect [Teaching]?
Answer: Because it is the person of the Perfect Teaching who receives the Dharma.
There is no dharma that is not perfect. Furthermore, as long as one has not yet attained the perfect understanding (*pariniṣpanna-adhigama*),
one should not rashly discuss cultivation and realization.
Even if one were to cultivate and realize [the truth],
one could not avoid the fact that days and kalpas multiply against one another; yet,
even when explaining the four teachings of the *Huafa* (Transformation Dharma), there is not even a single one among them.
What are these four?
They are the Tathāgata’s sublime wisdom for benefiting others,
which administers medicine in accordance with the illnesses of sentient beings.
When the affliction of thought is heavy,
the teaching of the Tripiṭaka is expounded for them; when the afflictions of both views and thought are light, [the Mahāyāna is taught].
For those with heavy afflictions of ignorance, he teaches the Shared Teaching; for others,
he teaches the Distinct Teaching.
For those whose illness of ignorance is light,
he preaches the Tripitaka Teaching and the Complete Teaching.
The four Āgamas constitute the Sūtra Piṭaka;
the Vinaya constitutes the Vinaya Piṭaka;
and the Abhidharma constitutes the Śāstra Piṭaka.
This teaching explains that within the four truths of arising and ceasing, suffering involves the transition through the three phases of birth, difference, and cessation;
origination involves the fluctuation of the four mental states, such as greed, hatred, delusion, and their equal combination;
and the path involves being easily supplanted by its counteractive factors.

When extinguished, existence ceases and returns to non-existence; this also explains the conceptualization of the arising and ceasing of the twelve links of dependent origination: ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness;
consciousness conditions name-and-form;
name-and-form conditions the six sense bases.
With the six sense bases as condition, contact arises;
with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises.
Clinging conditions grasping;
grasping conditions becoming;
becoming conditions birth.
With birth as condition, there are old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair.
With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease;
with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases.
With the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease.
With the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease.
With the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases.
With the cessation of contact, feeling ceases;
with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases;
with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases.
With the cessation of grasping, existence ceases;
with the cessation of existence, birth ceases;

with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction cease. This also explains the practice of the six perfections—generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—and it explains the real dharmas of the two truths, the aggregates, bases, and elements as conventional reality.
The actual existence of cessation is the true teaching for those of dull faculties within the realm of desire,
intended to lead them to cultivate the contemplation of analytical emptiness by observing the six elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness.
Free from the notions of self and what belongs to self, they emerge from the cycle of birth and death with limited segments and realize the partial, true nirvana;
this is the primary teaching for those of the two vehicles.
